extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and readers of Charles Lamb's essays/letters
extracted.subtask_description: Epistolary remarks and evaluative judgments by Charles Lamb on poetry, poetic style, and manners of criticism — informal guidance about what makes poetry (and criticism) effective or faulty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'the affected' style
rubrics_metrics.description: Beware falling into that mannered or self-conscious mode of writing which classical critics call 'the affected.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamb warns he began "to scent that I was getting into that sort of style which Longinus and Dionysius Halicarnassus fitly call 'the affected.'" Antipattern: rhetorical mannerisms and artificial ornament that draw attention to themselves rather than to the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid didactic sign-posting; do not tell readers how to feel
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not convey instructions or moral lessons so directly that they interrupt the reader's experience; avoid 'sign-posts' that say where the reader is to feel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamb: the fault in the 'Beggar' is that "the instructions conveyed in it are too direct, and like a lecture: they don't slide into the mind of the reader... An intelligent reader finds a sort of insult in being told, 'I will teach you how to think upon this subject.'" Guidance: let feeling and meaning emerge naturally from narrative and imagery rather than by explicit authorial instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles should not undermine a work's verisimilitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose titles that sustain, not weaken, the reader's suspension of belief or the work's claim to truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamb objects that calling the 'Ancient Mariner' a 'Poet's Reverie' is 'as bad as Bottom the Weaver's declaration that he is not a lion' — the title can be 'subversive of all credit' the tale should force upon us. Antipattern: labeling a narrative in a way that signals 'this is only a fancy' when the tale's power depends on seeming truthful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit unnecessary biographical specificity in certain tales
rubrics_metrics.description: For works that aim at the dreamlike, universal, or supernatural effect, withholding particulars of character and profession can heighten the story's power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamb defends not giving the 'Mariner' a profession or strong personal identity: the character 'undergoes such trials as overwhelm and bury all individuality' — in such cases, loss of personal detail contributes to the tale's universality and dreamlike quality. Use absence of specificity deliberately to produce dislocation or archetype.

rubrics_metrics.name: Praise with small qualifying exceptions to preserve sincerity
rubrics_metrics.description: When offering praise, inserting modest, trivial exceptions can remove the appearance of insincerity and increase the author's relish for the compliment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamb describes consoling Cottle by 'most unqualified praise, or only qualifying my praise by the occasional polite interposition of an exception taken against trivial faults' — this tactic makes praise feel more genuine. Guidance for critics: be candid but temper bluntness with tact when consoling; a little criticism amid praise can reinforce honesty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be bold in cutting during revision
rubrics_metrics.description: When editing, favor decisive excision — stronger cuts improve work more than timid half-measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamb: 'I perfectly accede to all your alterations, and only desire that you had cut deeper, when your hand was in.' Editorial guidance: do not shrink from removing material that weakens pace, focus, or tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overloading with sensational or excessive tropes
rubrics_metrics.description: Resist piling on an excess of horrors, marvels, or striking effects that fatigue the reader and dilute their impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On Cottle's epic Lamb complains of 'serpents, asps, spiders, ghosts, dead bodies, staircases made of nothing' and that 'He puts as many plums in his pudding as my grandmother used to do' — excessive, repetitive sensationalism lessens power and verisimilitude. Antipattern: cramming every terrifying image or grotesque device into long stretches without restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure foundational principles of criticism or argument are sound
rubrics_metrics.description: A work of criticism (or a prefatory argument) must rest on correct premises; a fundamentally wrong first principle can vitiate the whole reasoning that follows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamb recounts George Dyer discovering 'in the very first page of said Preface he had set out with a principle of criticism fundamentally wrong, which vitiated all his following reasoning.' Guidance: check and defend core assumptions before building extended argumentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid awkward archaisms and false idioms in diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not adopt unusual or archaic word-order or constructions that read as malapropistic or awkward unless intentionally stylistic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamb points out odd turns such as writing 'one a man' or 'he the king' as imitations that jar: 'two flowers of rhetoric palpably from the "Joan."' Guidance: prefer idiomatic clarity and avoid pastiche archaisms that feel unearned or distract the reader.
